t: in its time. At the times fixed by the Sages (see below halachah 4 onward).

and it is well known that this is an enactment of the prophets. This enactment was made in the days of Mordechai and Esther, when there were several prophets there (see Babylonian Talmud Megillah 14a, Jerusalem Talmud there 1:5).
and even kohanim at their service suspend their service. They stop their service in the Temple.
all are set aside for the reading of the Megillah. They first read the Megillah, and afterward perform the mitzvah.
except for a corpse with no one to bury it. Called a "met mitzvah" (see Hilchot Evel 3:8); because it lies in disgrace, they first bury it before the reading.
the one who encounters it. The one who finds it.
provided that he hears it from one who is obligated in its reading. For this principle see Hilchot Shofar 2:2.
all of it. From beginning to end.
at night and by day. Once at night and once by day.
the God who pleads our cause etc.. A blessing of thanksgiving that the Holy One, blessed be He, avenges the wrongs of Israel on its enemies.
a city. A town.

in which the miracle took place, as it says, "and rested on the fifteenth of it". As described in the Megillah, the Jews of Shushan fought their enemies on both the 13th and the 14th of Adar and rested from the fighting on the 15th, whereas in the other cities they fought only on the 13th and rested on the 14th. Because they fixed the day of Purim on the day of rest from the fighting, they equated all cities walled since the days of Joshua son of Nun with Shushan, which rested on the 15th, and equated unwalled cities with the other cities, which rested on the 14th.
in synagogues. Those in the villages.
on the day of assembly. The day on which they gather in the synagogue, so that they can read the Megillah with a minyan.
it is not read with fewer than ten. For the reason they enacted that they read early is so that they can read the Megillah with a minyan.

ten idlers who are permanently in the synagogue for public needs. Ten men who do not engage in labor, whose task is to remain in the synagogue for a mitzvah matter or other public needs (Commentary on the Mishnah, Megillah 1:3; in Responsa of the Rambam 123 he explained otherwise, and see Hamaspik le'Ovdei Hashem p. 112, that the Rambam retracted the view given in the responsum).
it is like a village. Because where there are no men available for a minyan, the minyan gathers on Monday and Thursday, like the villagers.

its repair is its damage. This town's being treated as a large city, reading on the fourteenth rather than at the special reading times, stems from its defect, that it does not have ten people, since even on the day of assembly it will not have a minyan (Kesef Mishneh; for this expression see also Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 1:7).

in what case does this apply... when Israel has a kingdom. And can compel observance of the mitzvot, so there is no concern that the villagers will neglect the reading of the Megillah (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Megillah 1:1).
a townsman. Whose time of reading is the 14th.
and a resident of a walled city. Whose time of reading is the 15th.

if he intended to return to his place at the time of reading. Of the place where he is now, and the determining time of reading is the time of the day, which is dawn. For example, a resident of a walled city who is in a town on the night of the fourteenth and intends to return to the walled city that night, so that he will be in the walled city at dawn, or a townsman who is in a walled city on the night of the fifteenth and intends to return to the town that night so that he will be in the town at dawn.
reads according to his own place. And does not read with the people of the place where he is now.

and if he did not intend to return until after the time of reading. Of the place where he is, for example a resident of a walled city who intends to stay on the night of the fourteenth in the town so that he will be there at dawn, or a townsman who intends to stay on the night of the fifteenth in the walled city so that he will be there at dawn (based on Kesef Mishneh, and see Piskim veShitot).

if there is no more than two thousand cubits between them, it is like a walled city. But if there is more than two thousand cubits between them, even if it is visible alongside it, it is not considered a walled city, and they read on the fourteenth.

and afterward the court intercalated the year. They added an extra month of Adar to it (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 4:1), and it is the determining month for reading the Megillah and the other mitzvot of the day (and compare below 2:13).
a decree. That the Sages decreed.
and let him go to one who is proficient in reading. So that he will read for him or teach him to read it (see also Hilchot Shofar, Sukkah, and Lulav 2:6, 7:13).
and carry it four cubits in the public domain. Which is one of the labors forbidden on Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 12:8).
out of order. Not in sequence.
and read the second verse for himself. The verse adjacent to the verse he forgot.
the foreign-language speaker. One who speaks a foreign language and does not understand the Holy Tongue.
in the Holy Tongue. In the Hebrew language.
and in the holy script. In Ashurit script letters.

and even if the listener was a Hebrew. One who understands the Holy Tongue but does not understand Greek fulfills his obligation in Greek (and see Hilchot Tefillin 1:19, that this language, as it was then, classical Greek, has been lost from the world).
provided that it is written in the script of that language. The script (font) of the letters must be that of the language in which the Megillah is written (based on Yad Peshutah).

but if it was written in Hebrew script and he read it in Aramaic to an Aramean etc.. It is not enough that the Megillah be written in Hebrew script and Hebrew language, for if at the time of reading he translates it into Aramaic, he is reading by heart and does not fulfill his obligation.
he was writing it, expounding it, or proofreading it. And while performing these actions, he read the verses of the Megillah aloud.
drowsing. Not awake, but not actually asleep (Hilchot Kriat Shema 2:12).
from the book from which he is copying while he writes. In which the entire Megillah is written.
and the adult reads it together with the minor. Together.
in the congregation. The shaliach tzibbur who reads to fulfill the congregation's obligation.
two read it. Together.
even ten have fulfilled their obligation as one. Unlike the Torah reading (see Hilchot Tefillah 12:11).

one does not read in the congregation from a Megillah written among the Writings. Because it is not evident that he is reading for the mitzvah of reading the Megillah, but rather as one reading Scripture in general, and there is no publicizing of the miracle.
longer or shorter than the other sheets. Longer or shorter than the other sheets.
so that it will have a distinguishing mark. That he is reading from it for the mitzvah of its reading.
but an individual reads from it. Because he knows that he is reading for the mitzvah of the Megillah.
on gevil or on klaf. Different kinds of processed hides used for writing a Torah scroll (see Hilchot Tefillin 1:6-8).
in gall-nut water. Water in which gall-nuts (growths on the oak or terebinth tree) were soaked, in which the ink is dissolved.
and kalkantos. Copper oxide which fixes the ink so that it is not easily erased.
tzivonin (colorants). Dyes (see there 1:4-5).
ruling. Before writing, they score the lines on the parchment with a knife, so that the writing will be straight (see there 1:12).
processing. Treatment.
a heretic. A denier of the faith.
if their impression is discernible. If the shape of the letters can be distinguished.
even if they were most of it. Of the Megillah.
until all its hides are one scroll. And not sheets separate from one another.
with sinews, like a Torah scroll. Sinews of a kosher domestic or wild animal (see Hilchot Sefer Torah 9:13).
and he need not sew the entire sheet like a scroll etc.. That is, the sheets are sewn to one another along their whole length except for a small portion at the top and bottom (see there 9:14).
because it is called an iggeret (letter). As it says in it, "all the words of this letter" (Esther 9:26), "to confirm this letter of Purim" (ibid. 9:29), and it is not called a "sefer" (book).
the ten sons of Haman and the word "the ten" in one breath. The list of the ten sons of Haman and also the word "aseret" (the ten) written at its end (Esther 9:7-10).

he reads and spreads it open like a letter etc.. He begins reading while it is still rolled, and during his reading he spreads the Megillah open like a letter and does not roll it up until the end of the reading.
villagers who read early etc.. As explained above 1:6-7.
and they are forbidden on these two days. On the 14th and 15th.
and if he does not have. When he does not have enough food both for himself and to send to his friend.
and one is not particular about Purim money. To check whether the person is a poor man fit to receive charity or not.
Purim money. Money meant to be distributed to the poor on the day of Purim.

he is likened to the Shechinah, as it says, "to revive the spirit of the lowly and to revive the heart of the crushed". The beginning of the verse says: "For thus says the High and Exalted One who dwells forever and whose name is holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and with the crushed and lowly of spirit," teaching us that the occupation of the Holy One, blessed be He, is encouraging the poor and wretched, and one who does so behaves in the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He.

all memory of the troubles will be annulled, as it says, "for the former troubles are forgotten". Further on there it says: "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered..." The prophet describes that the goodness of the righteous in the days of the Messiah will cause the troubles of the past to be forgotten.
in the Second Temple. In the days of the Second Temple.
and annulled their religion. Prevented them from observing their religion.
and laid hands on their money and their daughters. Plundered their property and violated their daughters.
and entered the Sanctuary. Of the Temple.
and made breaches in it. Made holes in the lattice fence surrounding the Temple (see Mishnah Middot 2:3).
until the second destruction. Until the destruction of the Second Temple.
pure oil. That had not been defiled by the Greeks.
and there was in it only enough to light for one day. The quantity of oil in it was enough for only one day.
the lamps of the arrangement. The lamps that the kohen arranges in the Temple menorah.
until they pressed olives. In purity.
and because of this. That the oil lasted for eight days.
with eulogy and fasting. With a eulogy and a fast, public or individual (see also Hilchot Evel 11:3, Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:7, 1:9).
like the days of Purim. See above 2:13.
a mitzvah from the words of the Scribes. From the words of the Sages.
like the reading of the Megillah. See above 1:1.
whoever is obligated in the reading of the Megillah. See above 1:1.
and anyone who sees it. Even if he already recited the blessing and lit in his own home (see Responsa of the Rambam 228).
they complete the Hallel. They recite all of it.
whether an individual or a congregation. Whether an individual recites it or the congregation recites it.
in the way that one blesses over the Megillah. See above 1:3.
and over the eruv. See Hilchot Eruvin 1:16.
for every certainty of their words. That the Sages obligated, not because of doubt.
and the main reason they made it for him. The reason for his enactment.
tithe of demai. Produce from which one tithes because of doubt that it was not tithed (see Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1).

the second festival day. The day that those outside the Land of Israel add to every festival. When the month was intercalated in the Land of Israel on the basis of sighting, those outside the Land did not know the date on which the month was fixed and observed two festival days out of doubt, and they enacted that even now, when the sanctification is by calculation, they continue to observe so (Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:4-6; and see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:21).
the eight days of the festival. Sukkot and Shemini Atzeret.
and the day of Atzeret. Shavuot.
places that observe festivals for two days. For the details of the places see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:11.
a custom and not a mitzvah. Not even from the words of the Scribes.
they read with skipping. As detailed in the next halachah.
and one who reads the Hallel out of order. Who read it not in sequence.
even though he waited long enough to finish all of it. That he waited a length of time sufficient for reading the whole Hallel (compare above 2:2, Hilchot Kriat Shema 2:12).
he may interrupt. By speaking (and compare the laws of interruption in the Shema and its blessings, Hilchot Kriat Shema 2:15-16).
they double each and every thing. Each and every verse.
both women. Who are also obligated in the mitzvah (see above 3:4).
he lights ten lamps etc.. The householder lights the number of lamps that is added each day, and as many as there are members of the household.
a lamp that has two mouths. A clay lamp with two spouts, each with a wick.
it serves two people. Each spout can serve as a separate lamp for one person.
he filled a bowl with oil and surrounded it with wicks. And the wicks are placed on the sides of the bowl, distant from one another.
if he inverted a vessel over it etc.. By inverting the vessel, each wick is distinct by itself and is considered a lamp by itself.
if he did not invert a vessel over it, it becomes like a bonfire. For the flames are considered mixed together.
and it is not counted even as one lamp. For the mitzvah is specifically with a lamp, and not with a bonfire.
at its setting. At the time of sunset.
until the foot leaves the marketplace. Until passersby stop passing in the street.
if this time has passed, he does not light. For since there are no people in the street, there is no publicizing of the miracle.
he lit it and it went out, he need not light it again. Even if it went out immediately, because the lighting is the mitzvah (below halachah 9).

even though the oils do not draw after the wick and the fire does not take hold well in those wicks. In contrast to the Shabbat lamp, which one may not light with such oils and wicks, for fear that he will tilt the lamp on Shabbat so that it burns better (Hilchot Shabbat 5:5-11).
because it is forbidden to make use of the Chanukah light, whether on Shabbat or on a weekday. And therefore there is no concern that he will tilt the lamp.
even to examine coins or to count them by its light. For even slight use is forbidden.
at the door of the house, on the outside. In order to publicize the miracle.
and if he lived in an upper story. And has no open door onto the public domain.
in days of danger. When it is not possible to light the Chanukah lamp outside.
it suffices for him. It is enough for him, and he has fulfilled the mitzvah.
for the one who sees says, "he is standing here for his own needs". And it is not evident that he lit for the sake of the mitzvah.
an ashashit. A vessel with a lamp inside, made for light.
at the close of Shabbat he extinguishes it, blesses, and lights it. And he fulfills his obligation with it, even though it was placed there for another purpose.
and it is permitted to light a Chanukah lamp from another Chanukah lamp. Even though it is forbidden to use a Chanukah lamp for other things (see above halachah 6).
on two sides. In two directions.
so that those passing on that side will not say etc.. People passing on the side on which he did not light will think that the householder did not light at all.
a guest for whom they light in his house. For example his father, wife, or grown sons.
has no house in which to light for himself. That there is no one who will light for him in his house, or he has no house.
and he joins with them in the oil. In the expense of paying for the oil, so that he will have a share in the mitzvah.
and if he had a house of his own. In the place where he is staying.
because of the passersby. So that they will not suspect him of not having lit.
even if he has nothing to eat but from charity. That he is poor and supported by charity.
his garment. His clothing.

the sanctification of Shabbat. That one must sanctify the Shabbat day at its entrance (Hilchot Shabbat 29:1), and from the words of the Scribes that this Kiddush be made over a cup of wine (ibid. 29:6).
he gives precedence to oil for lighting a Chanukah lamp over wine for the sanctification of the day. It is preferable that he buy oil for the Chanukah lamps rather than wine for Kiddush of the day.
if he had before him the lamp of his house etc.. That he had money for only one of them.
the lamp of his house. The Shabbat lamp, which it is a mitzvah from the words of the Scribes to light, and which is part of the delight of Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 5:1).
for the sake of peace in his home. So that his house will not be dark without a lamp.

for behold, the Name is erased to make peace between a man and his wife. For in the sotah procedure the kohen would erase into the water a scroll on which God's Name was written (see Hilchot Sotah 3:8-10).
for the entire Torah was given. This is the purpose of the giving of the Torah.
